solutions from adjacent time steps for initializing new frames. As a
result, manual and semi-automatic tracking methods have been noted
to require multiple hours or days of human effort to fully process a
single trial [39]. These drawbacks limit scalability of precise tracking
workflows in research and clinical settings.
The current work introduces a system for fully automatic tracking
of native joint kinematics in high-speed stereo-radiography (HSSR)
sequences [41]. The proposed method consists of three distinct computational steps. Radiographs are first annotated with segmentation
maps and semantic key points using convolutional neural networks
(CNNs). Next, initial bone pose estimates are computed using subjectspecific surface landmarks and CNN-predicted key points. Initial poses
are then refined by registering CT-based DRRs to masked radiographs.
A particular CNN architecture is also proposed which exploits subjectspecific surface models for improved radiograph annotation; and a
biplanar Perspective-n-Point (PnP) formulation is solved using semidefinite relaxations to obtain reliable, preliminary pose estimates. The
introduced approach is applied to track native shoulder kinematics,
in which observed radiographs are characterized by low contrast and
heavy occlusions by surrounding tissue and bone. Predicted GH kinematics are evaluated by comparing to manually tracked values from
17 trials capturing 4 distinct activities performed by living individuals.
Observed differences routinely within 2.0◦ for 2 out of 3 joint-level
DoFs demonstrate the viability of end-to-end automation of kinematic
tracking in stereo-radiography sequences.

refinement. Burton et al. [52] implemented a similar approach to track
native knee kinematics in stereo-radiography. Initial pose estimates
were obtained from a biplanar PnP formulation solved with block
coordinate descent, and pose refinement was performed by registering
surface models to masked radiographs. Gu et al. [53] proposed a
CNN architecture to predict initial poses from encoded radiographs
and DRRs. Recently, Jensen et al. [54] predicted preliminary implant
poses in single plane radiography by matching CNN-segmented implant contours to predefined libraries of normalized Fourier descriptors
(NFD) [17]. Poses were then refined using global optimization to
estimate precise TKA kinematics. These previous investigations adopted
a multi-stage framework characterized by three distinct steps including preliminary image annotation with machine learning, initial pose
estimation, and pose refinement. The current work also adheres to
this multi-stage framework but builds upon previous investigations
in two key ways. A CNN architecture is proposed which leverages
subject-specific geometric data to inform segmentation predictions, and
a semidefinite relaxation strategy is implemented to obtain globally
optimal preliminary pose estimates from a non-convex biplanar PnP
formulation. The current investigation also reports results for automatic
tracking of native GH kinematics, a challenging task in which radiographs are characterized by low contrast and significant occlusions.
Results for this target application have been so far unreported.

2. Related work

The emergence of large-scale CNNs has prompted development of
robust machine learning (ML) models that perform a wide range of
computer vision tasks. Two prevalent tasks include automatic segmentation [55–57] and semantic key point prediction [58–60]. Automatic
segmentation is characterized by pixel-wise annotation of query images
to delineate object boundaries while semantic key point prediction
involves annotating scenes with 2D landmarks of interest. ML models
have been applied to annotate radiograph frames for various purposes
with promising results [52,54,61–64].
While CNN architectures have classically been composed of affine
transformations and non-linear activations [65–67], recent work has
also aimed to augment models with a wider range of operators for
enhanced expressivity [68,69]. A precondition for these introduced
operators is that they should be analytically differentiable to allow
backpropagation and end-to-end training. Numerical optimization as an
embedded operator has been identified as one candidate for improving
expressivity of ML models [70–73]. Specifically, computing analytical
gradients of optimization solutions with respect to learned input data
has enabled solving numerical optimization problems during an architecture’s forward pass, while also allowing backpropagation through
optimization modules. Gradients have been derived by solving systems
of equations based on Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, or with
the Implicit Function Theorem [74,75].
A particular instantiation of this emerging class of differentiable
modules is backpropagatable PnP, in which gradients of optimized
poses can be computed with respect to input data [76,77]. Differentiable rendering has also been introduced as a backpropagatable
module that can augment ML architectures. While the rasterization
step of conventional computer graphics prevents computing analytical
gradients, differentiable reformulations have enabled backpropagation
through rendered images with respect to scene parameters, including
pose [78–81]. As will be shown, the current work adopts these advanced differentiable modules as part of a CNN architecture which uses
subject-specific geometric data to inform radiograph annotations.

2.2. Deep learning for computer vision

2.1. Model-image registration
Early methods for accelerating model-image registration utilized
semi-automatic frameworks. These approaches applied numerical optimization algorithms to minimize loss functions which quantify similarities between radiograph frames and dynamically rendered images. Loss
functions have also been augmented with regularization terms [42] or
simulated contact and ligament force constraints [29,43] to mitigate
spurious local minima known to exist in the induced loss landscapes.
Otake et al. [44] investigated the use of Covariance Matrix AdaptationEvolutionary Strategies (CMA-ES) to register the proximal femur with
CT-based DRRs. An intensity-based similarity metric was computed
at multiple scales using progressively increasing radiograph and DRR
resolutions. Mahfouz et al. [20] combined simulated annealing and
Nelder–Mead simplex to register total knee arthroplasty (TKA) components by accounting for intensity and contour differences between
projection maps and radiographs. Flood and Banks [8] introduced a
global optimization algorithm based on hierarchical division of search
space hyper-rectangles to acquire TKA kinematics from single plane
fluoroscopy. Implant component poses were estimated by penalizing
differences between post-processed radiograph contours and surface
mesh projection maps. These methods utilized gradient-free optimization or relied on numerical gradients. More recent investigations have
sought to develop methods based on analytical gradients [45,46].
Gopalakrishnan and Golland [47] implemented DRR rendering as a
series of backpropagatable tensor operations to compute analytical gradients of a similarity metric with respect to scene pose. An alternative
approach used neural nets to regress to pose from intensity residual
maps constructed from rendered implants and radiograph frames [48].
In contrast to these previous investigations, the current work develops
methods for fully automatic bone pose estimation.

ABSTRACT
The current work introduces a system for fully automatic tracking of native glenohumeral kinematics in
stereo-radiography sequences. The proposed method first applies convolutional neural networks to obtain
segmentation and semantic key point predictions in biplanar radiograph frames. Preliminary bone pose
estimates are computed by solving a non-convex optimization problem with semidefinite relaxations to register
digitized bone landmarks to semantic key points. Initial poses are then refined by registering computed
tomography-based digitally reconstructed radiographs to captured scenes, which are masked by segmentation
maps to isolate the shoulder joint. A particular neural net architecture which exploits subject-specific geometry
is also introduced to improve segmentation predictions and increase robustness of subsequent pose estimates.
The method is evaluated by comparing predicted glenohumeral kinematics to manually tracked values from
17 trials capturing 4 dynamic activities. Median orientation differences between predicted and ground truth
poses were 1.7◦ and 8.6◦ for the scapula and humerus, respectively. Joint-level kinematics differences were
less than 2◦ in 65%, 13%, and 63% of frames for XYZ orientation DoFs based on Euler angle decompositions.
Automation of kinematic tracking can increase scalability of tracking workflows in research, clinical, or surgical
applications.

1. Introduction
Model-image registration enables precise tracking of in vivo jointlevel kinematics in radiograph sequences in biomechanics and orthopaedics methods [1–5]. Also referred to as 2D-3D registration, this
procedure involves estimating 6-degree of freedom (6-DoF) poses of
objects observed in radiographs by comparing captured frames to dynamically rendered images of digitized models. Scenes are iteratively
generated as a function of pose to find configurations which replicate the appearances and shapes of target objects in original radiographs. Rendered images are instantiated as digitally reconstructed
radiographs (DRRs) or surface model perspective projections [6–8],
acquired from computed tomography (CT) scans [9,10] or magnetic
resonance imaging (MRI) [11–13].
Individual object poses estimated with model-image registration
are represented with respect to semantically relevant coordinate systems and aggregated to recover joint-level kinematics [14–16]. Modelimage registration has been successfully applied to compute kinematics
of the native or implanted knee [1,2,4,17–21], shoulder [3,13,22–
26], spine [27,28], and other joints [29,30] from single plane [17]

or biplanar systems [2,4]. In particular, previous studies evaluated
glenohumeral (GH) kinematics differences between dominant and nondominant joints [31], or compared healthy to injured or implanted
shoulders [32–35].
Kinematic tracking in radiographs has most commonly been performed manually or semi-automatically. Manual tracking requires that
trained observers iteratively specify multiple poses until rendered images of target objects are sufficiently similar to captured radiographs.
In contrast, semi-automatic methods compare radiograph frames to
rendered images using scalar-valued objective functions, and invoke
numerical optimization to minimize such objectives as a function of
pose. A wide range of objective functions [36–38] and optimization
methods [29,39,40] have been employed in prior work, and have
contributed a degree of automation to the tracking process. However,
a stipulation of semi-automatic methods is that object poses must be
carefully initialized within just a few millimeters (mm) or degrees of
the true pose to cope with chaotic loss landscapes and expensive rendering operations [20,40]. Pose iterates are also susceptible to settling
in undesirable local minima, and this may preclude the use of pose

2. Related work

The emergence of large-scale CNNs has prompted development of
robust machine learning (ML) models that perform a wide range of

segmentation is characterized by pixel-wise annotation of query images

pose [78–81]. As will be shown, the current work adopts these advanced differentiable modules as part of a CNN architecture which uses

Background: Dynamic radiographic measurements of 3-dimensional (3-D) total knee arthroplasty (TKA)
kinematics have provided important information for implant design and surgical technique for over 30
years. However, current methods of measuring TKA kinematics are too cumbersome, inaccurate, or timeconsuming for practical clinical application. Even state-of-the-art techniques require human-supervision
to obtain clinically reliable kinematics. Eliminating human supervision could potentially make this
technology practical for clinical use.
Methods: We demonstrate a fully autonomous pipeline for quantifying 3D-TKA kinematics from singleplane radiographic imaging. First, a convolutional neural network (CNN) segmented the femoral and
tibial implants from the image. Second, those segmented images were compared to precomputed shape
libraries for initial pose estimates. Lastly, a numerical optimization routine aligned 3D implant contours
and ﬂuoroscopic images to obtain the ﬁnal implant poses.
Results: The autonomous technique reliably produces kinematic measurements comparable to humansupervised measures, with root-mean-squared differences of less than 0.7 mm and 4 for our test
data, and 0.8 mm and 1.7 for external validation studies.
Conclusion: A fully autonomous method to measure 3D-TKA kinematics from single-plane radiographic
images produces results equivalent to a human-supervised method, and may soon make it practical to
perform these measurements in a clinical setting.

The current work introduces a method for fully automatic tracking of native knee kinematics from stereoradiography sequences. The framework consists of three computational steps. First, biplanar radiograph frames
are annotated with segmentation maps and key points using a convolutional neural network. Next, initial

the global minimum of the non-convex problem. Pose estimates are then refined by registering computed

also introduced which enables generating digitally reconstructed radiographs from computed tomography scans
with inconsistent slice widths. The automatic tracking framework was evaluated with stereo-radiography trials
manually tracked with model-image registration, and with frames which capture a synthetic leg phantom.

in phantom trials. Results indicate the described framework may benefit orthopaedics and biomechanics
applications through acceleration of kinematic tracking.

1. Introduction
In vivo measurement of native knee kinematics from stereoradiography enables non-invasive evaluation of patient-specific movement. Kinematic tracking is performed with model-image registration
(or 2D–3D registration), which incorporates digitized anatomic models
in a computer graphics framework to estimate 6-degree of freedom
(6-DoF) poses of objects observed in radiographs (Hamilton et al.,
2022; Lu et al., 2008; Myers et al., 2012). Surface meshes or digitally
reconstructed radiographs (DRRs) are dynamically rendered at multiple
query poses to find perspective projections that replicate the shapes and
appearances of target structures in captured frames. Joint-level kinematics are then reconstructed from estimated bone poses to quantify
motion observed during dynamic activities (Grood and Suntay, 1983;
Tashman et al., 2004). This framework has been extensively used to assess kinematic differences across multiple activities and groups (Hamai
et al., 2009; Kefala et al., 2017; Kozanek et al., 2009; Seisler and
Sheehan, 2007; Qi et al., 2013), and to drive high-fidelity simulations

in computational biomechanics (Martelli et al., 2020; Navacchia et al.,
2019). An understanding of healthy kinematic profiles can also inform
surgical factors or implant designs with regards to orthopaedic surgery,
as recovery of normal kinematics is a primary concern (Akbari Shandiz
et al., 2016; Ishikawa et al., 2015; Kitagawa et al., 2010; Lustig et al.,
2021).
Previous work has demonstrated the accuracy of model-image registration (Anderst et al., 2009; Giphart et al., 2012; Postolka et al.,
2020; You et al., 2001), but conventional tracking procedures are
prohibitive. Manually tracking a single patient activity is an arduous
process requiring multiple hours or days of effort by trained annotators
using interactive software (Prins et al., 2015). Numerical optimization
has benefited tracking by refining user-provided poses through minimization of cost functions (Hoff et al., 1998; Mahfouz et al., 2003;
Mu, 2010; Zuffi et al., 1999). However, this semi-automatic approach
requires initial pose estimates within just a few millimeters (mm) or
degrees of an object’s true pose. Consequently, kinematic tracking is

refinement and was evaluated by comparing predicted kinematics to
manually tracked values. A limitation of surface mesh rendering is its
inability to capture volumetric material property data, which benefits
pose refinement by revealing cortical bone contours in dynamically
rendered images. Material property information can be incorporated
during pose refinement by rendering DRRs from computed tomography
(CT) data. However, efficient DRR rendering algorithms assume availability of CT scans with consistent slice widths (Jacobs et al., 1998;
Siddon, 1985), and this assumption is routinely violated in practice.
CT scans captured for knee tracking applications consist of finer slice
widths near the joint and thicker slices along the femoral and tibial
shafts. This practical consideration complicates the use of efficient DRR
algorithms during pose refinement.
The current work investigates fully automatic tracking of native
knee kinematics from stereo-radiography sequences. A multi-stage
framework is described which consists of image annotation, initial pose
estimation, and pose refinement. Although a previous study reported
results for a similar application, the current work presents multiple
technical and methodological contributions. First, initial pose estimates
are acquired by globally solving a non-convex polynomial optimization
problem with semidefinite relaxations. This approach mitigates poor
initial pose estimates corresponding to local minima arising from nonconvexity of the problem. Next, a DRR rendering algorithm is presented
which supports generating DRRs from CT scans composed of variable
slice widths. This rendering method enables use of full lower body
CT scans during pose refinement while obviating the need for nonhomogeneous CT voxel resampling. Finally, the tracking framework is
extensively evaluated against in vivo kinematics manually tracked by
trained experts, and with additional trials capturing a bead-implanted
phantom. It was hypothesized that the tracking framework would produce accurate pose estimates; with better agreement between predicted
and reference values expected in phantom frames than in manually
tracked trials.

(CT) data. However, efficient DRR rendering algorithms assume availability of CT scans with consistent slice widths (Jacobs et al., 1998;
Siddon, 1985), and this assumption is routinely violated in practice.
CT scans captured for knee tracking applications consist of finer slice
widths near the joint and thicker slices along the femoral and tibial
shafts. This practical consideration complicates the use of efficient DRR
algorithms during pose refinement.
The current work investigates fully automatic tracking of native
knee kinematics from stereo-radiography sequences. A multi-stage
framework is described which consists of image annotation, initial pose
estimation, and pose refinement. Although a previous study reported
results for a similar application, the current work presents multiple
technical and methodological contributions. First, initial pose estimates
are acquired by globally solving a non-convex polynomial optimization
problem with semidefinite relaxations. This approach mitigates poor
initial pose estimates corresponding to local minima arising from nonconvexity of the problem. Next, a DRR rendering algorithm is presented
which supports generating DRRs from CT scans composed of variable
slice widths. This rendering method enables use of full lower body
CT scans during pose refinement while obviating the need for nonhomogeneous CT voxel resampling. Finally, the tracking framework is
extensively evaluated against in vivo kinematics manually tracked by
trained experts, and with additional trials capturing a bead-implanted
phantom. It was hypothesized that the tracking framework would produce accurate pose estimates; with better agreement between predicted
and reference values expected in phantom frames than in manually
tracked trials.

for measuring cup position in total hip arthroplasty

James A. Sullivan3,4 · Michael I. Solomon5 · Eric M. Slotkin6

· Qing Li2 · Catherine Z. Stambouzou1 ·

Received: 20 May 2024 / Accepted: 8 April 2025
© CARS 2025

Abstract
Purpose This study evaluated the accuracy of an automated 2D–3D registration software for matching preoperative 3D
models of the pelvis and acetabular component to intraoperative 2D fluoroscopy images in total hip arthroplasty (THA).
Methods We developed a 2D–3D registration software that registers a 3D model of the pelvis from preoperative CT and a
3D model of the acetabular implant to intraoperative fluoroscopic imaging, thereby calculating the implant position relative to
the 3D pelvic reference frame. A total of 145 datasets were used including 65 digitally reconstructed radiographs, 20 dry bone
phantoms datasets and 60 clinical datasets with preoperative CT and intraoperative fluoroscopy imaging. Achieved acetabular
positions from the clinical images were determined from post-operative CT using a 3D/3D registration method. Accuracy
was assessed by comparing the calculated acetabular position from the 2D–3D software to the ground truth data.
Results Mean absolute difference between ground truth and the 2D–3D software was 1.9° [signed error range: −4.4, 4.8]
for inclination, 1.5° [−7.3, 4.1] for anteversion, 1.6 mm [−5, 3.8] for cup height and 1.8 mm [−7.3, 4.1] for depth across all
datasets. In total, 100% of inclination results and 98% of anteversion results were within 5° while 90% of height and 81% of
depth results were within 3 mm.
Conclusion We validated the accuracy of an automated 2D–3D registration software for use in THA. While our method
requires preoperative data from CT, the results are comparable to robotics and image-based navigation, and present a promising,
simple technology that can be easily integrated into an operating room for THA.

component placement and has been shown to improve the
accuracy of placing an acetabular component within the
Lewinnek safe zone [3–5]. However, the two-dimensional
nature of IF can result in inaccuracy, due in part to incorrect
assumptions of the patient’s pelvic tilt which alters true component positioning values, and the variability of the pelvic tilt
between the measurement taken with the patient lying down
and that on the traction table that is often used in DAA [6–9].
Techniques exist to reduce the error from pelvic positioning
in fluoroscopic images (allowing for 2D–2D comparisons
with preoperative patient radiographs); however, they often
require manual manipulation of the C-arm’s beam direction to recreate the preoperative anteroposterior (AP) X-ray

123

 International Journal of Computer Assisted Radiology and Surgery

patient position [3, 10]. Additionally, they utilize accepted
guidelines that require surgeons to replicate quantitative measures through qualitative approaches. For example, a true
AP radiograph has a coccyx to pubic symphysis distance
of between 1 and 3 cm, with surgeons visually estimating
the distance on an X-ray [11]. Further evaluation of these
techniques when utilized to assess acetabular component orientation demonstrated less accuracy and was often unreliable
due to patient-specific morphologies [12]. Brush et al. also
found that surgeons relying solely on IF for the estimation of
cup anteversion and inclination were unreliable [13].
2D–3D registration has been proposed as a technique to
improve the accuracy of measuring component position after
THA [14–17]. While 2D–3D registration has been investigated for registering preoperative CT scans [18–20] or 3D
statistical shape models [14] to 2D X-ray and mobile radiographs after THA, few algorithms have been developed and
evaluated for use with IF and those that have been commercialized require multiple shots for a single registration, a
point-based matching method for initial registration and invasive trackers pinned in the pelvis [21]. Fluoroscopy images
are more commonly used intraoperatively over traditional Xrays and have smaller and often varying fields of view and
image quality, as well as reversed image intensities. Therefore, it is important that 2D–3D registration algorithms are
robust enough to be used with such images. Yamada et al.
reported on the accuracy of a 2D–3D CT-based navigation
system for THA; however, this system required optical trackers to be attached to pelvis using invasive bone pins and
to the acetabular inserter handle to determine the position
of the acetabular implant relative to the bone [21]. Novel
software platforms are now actively being developed to use
2D–3D registration for component measurements and positioning using IF without requiring invasive bone trackers and
pins. This study aims to assess the accuracy of a novel, automated 2D–3D registration technique and software to measure
acetabular cup positions using IF. Our hypothesis was that
accuracy would be within 2 degrees and 2 mm mean absolute error (MAE) for cup inclination, anteversion, height
and medialization across a range of simulated and actual IF
images.

Methods and materials
2D–3D registration software
We developed a fully automated 2D–3D registration method
that rigidly aligns the known 3D pelvis geometry obtained
from preoperative CT and a cup implant surface model to
a given single-plane intraoperative 2D fluoroscopy image
showing the hip joint. As inputs, the method reads the patientspecific CT and pelvis surface with known patient-specific

123

3D landmark locations, a 3D surface model of the implant
to be registered, the 2D IF image, as well as preoperative
information about the planned alignment of cup and pelvis.
The method then computes the relative 3D orientation and
position of the pelvis and cup as depicted in the IF image,
making use of the known calibration parameters (source–detector distance and pixel size) of the C-arm used for obtaining
the image. The position of the final cup is determined by registering a virtual 3D model of the cup to the cup in the 2D
images. Once computed, the 3D transformations of pelvis and
cup are applied to derive clinical measurements of the artificial joint construct such as the current cup inclination and
anteversion relative to the anterior pelvic plane (APP). The
measurement of inclination with respect to the APP is defined
as the angle between a line on the APP that is perpendicular
to the line between the left and right anterior superior iliac
spine (ASIS) points and runs through the midpoint between
the pubic symphyses and the cup axis projected onto the APP.
Anteversion is defined as the line between the cup axis and
the APP. The measurement of ML (depth) and SI cup position
is taken by projecting the cup centre on the APP, with ML
measured along the direction of the ASIS’s and SI perpendicular to ML. On the screen, the surgeon can visualize the
semicircular appearance of the cup implant superimposed on
the 2D IF images, as well as the anteversion and inclination
values.

Excellent — Jensen 2023 has rich detail:

1. **Pipeline**: CNN segmentation → NFD shape library initial pose (projections with ±30° out-of-plane rotation at 3° increments) → DIRECT-JTA optimization refinement. "the leaf branch served to find the optimal out-of-plane translation" — confirming the DIRECT-JTA leaf = z-search stage.
2. **Tibia ambiguity**: "Transversely symmetric tibial implants posed problems during registration because 2 distinct poses produced roughly identical projections [50]. Because of this pose ambiguity, the tibial implant was always optimized after the nonsymmetric femoral implant and included additional mediolateral translation and varus/valgus rotation penalties." — the DIRECT lineage of JTML's "tibia-after-femur" + pole constraints! The "ambiguous zone" (AZ) concept.
3. **Accuracy (final kinematics vs human-supervised)**: in-plane translations < 0.8 mm RMS; out-of-plane < 1.8 mm; rotations ≤ 4° inside ambiguous zone, < 1.7° outside. Test data < 0.7 mm & 4°; external validation 0.8 mm & 1.7°.
4. **Blunder definition**: squared sum of rotation differences > 5°.
5. **Out-of-plane translation is the worst axis**: "the out-of-plane translation estimates were relatively poor for both ground-truth projections and CNN-segmented images. This translation estimate is extremely sensitive to model projection and edge detection details and can be adjusted for better results if required." And "Due to poor sensitivity for measuring out-of-plane translation with monocular vision, the medio-lateral translation had the largest RMS differences for both image types." — field-confirmed z-weak axis in the DIRECT-JTA lineage itself!
6. **External validation**: 45 single-plane images instrumented sawbones with motion capture; 260 single-plane image pairs from a biplane TKA study; all in-plane translation errors submillimeter except S/I from biplane study; all rotation errors < 1.8°.

The numbers to use as external benchmarks for the ablation runner:
- Jensen 2023 (JTML, single-plane, DIRECT-JTA + ML init): in-plane < 0.8 mm RMS, out-of-plane < 1.8 mm RMS, rotations < 1.7° (outside AZ) / ≤ 4° (inside AZ).
- Flood 2018 (DIRECT-JTA, single-plane, manual init): strict success = within 1 mm in-plane + 1° rotations; out-of-plane excluded from success; average out-of-plane error ~1 mm for femur at capture-range trials (femoral "average out-of-plane translation around one millimeter").
- Arulampalam 2025 (THA cup, single-plane intraop fluoro): MAE 1.9° incl, 1.5° antev, 1.6 mm height, 1.8 mm depth.
- Burton 2023 (biplanar native glenohumeral): median orientation 1.7° (scapula) / 8.6° (humerus).
- Burton 2024 (biplanar native knee): <1.0 mm and <1.0° for all DoFs in phantom trials.

The key external-benchmark story for the ablation runner: JTML should report per-axis translation/rotation errors against these field numbers, with the honest expectation that z is the weak axis everywhere (Yamazaki 2.6 mm conventional, Jensen 1.8 mm out-of-plane, Arulampalam 1.8 mm depth).

Now, the perturbation-suite question (#4): does any corpus paper report gate-like sensitivity analysis that the suite should mirror? 
- Flood 2018 Table V: dilation sensitivity — femur robust trunk dilation 8-12, tibia 4-8 (Group A), 6-8 (Group B). Also Table VI: Canny threshold sensitivity (noisy/insufficient edge detection). This is exactly the "gate-like sensitivity analysis" — Flood perturbed the dilation constant ±1 and ±2 from high-performance values and measured success-rate robustness. The JTML perturbation suite should mirror this: dilations {6,3,1} are at the edge of Flood's robust range for femur (8-12) — a real finding! JTML's trunk dilation 6 is BELOW the femur-robust 8-12 range.
- Jensen 2023: ambiguous zone analysis (tibia rotations, 4° threshold).
- Yamazaki 2004: evaluation curves per variable (the sensitivity curves).

Also, the Yamazaki polynomial-fit remedy directly maps onto our z-profile probe + polish: JTML's polish stage (angle 06) chamfer valley-depth gate G1-G4 is a modern version of Yamazaki's independent z optimization. And Yamazaki's "10 sample points" is exactly a 10-point z-sweep with polynomial fit — the probe's valley_depth metric on a 31-point sweep is the same instrument with better sampling.

  (c) "coupling mode": probe the z-profile at the RECOVERED in-plane pose (not only fem.jts truth) — Yamazaki's residual bias shows in-plane error shifts the z extremum; the probe measures the coupling slope dz*/d(in-plane) by re-running the sweep at ±the minimal-detectable-regression in-plane Δ. This upgrades p4 (z_gap anti-correlates with valley_depth) with a mechanism.
- z-remedies question (synthesis): the field's documented z remedies are now enumerated — (1) decoupled z-polish (Yamazaki, 2.6→0.9 mm), (2) biplane (Flood: "An orthogonal biplane comparison is likely the best resolution", Yamazaki: accurate but space/complexity/radiation), (3) known-geometry prior (Yamazaki: conventional practice set medio-lateral to zero — JTML already pins tibia/femur relative pose from .jts), (4) penalized z (Jensen: "additional mediolateral translation and varus/valgus rotation penalties" for the tibia — the pole-constraint family's field precedent). All four are now corpus-backed; the probe + ablation decide which to pursue on JTML's geometry.

#### R3-3 — State-of-the-art benchmarks: per-axis external error tables for the ablation runner's reports

Table-ish list:
- Jensen 2023 (single-plane TKA, DIRECT-JTA + CNN/NFD init; RMS vs human-supervised): in-plane translations < 0.8 mm; out-of-plane < 1.8 mm; rotations < 1.7° outside ambiguous zone / ≤ 4° inside; external validation (45 sawbones motion-capture frames + 260 biplane-derived single-plane pairs): all in-plane translation errors sub-millimeter (except S/I), all rotation errors < 1.8°; blunder = squared-sum rotation diff > 5°.
- Flood 2018 (single-plane TKA, DIRECT-JTA): strict success = in-plane ≤ 1 mm AND rotations ≤ 1° (out-of-plane explicitly excluded); femoral average out-of-plane ~1 mm at convergence-range trials; capture range ±55 mm/deg femur, ±25-40 tibia.
- Yamazaki 2004: z 2.6→0.9 mm sim / 3.2→1.4 mm in vitro; other 5 DOF SD ~0.1 mm / ~0.2-0.3°.
- Arulampalam 2025 (single-plane intraop fluoro THA cup, automated): MAE 1.9° inclination [−4.4,4.8], 1.5° anteversion [−7.3,4.1], 1.6 mm height [−5,3.8], 1.8 mm depth [−7.3,4.1]; 100%/98% within 5° (incl/antev), 90% height within 3 mm, 81% depth within 3 mm — depth is the weakest axis even in a 2025 commercial-lineage automated product.
- Burton 2023 (biplanar native GH): median orientation 1.7° scapula / 8.6° humerus vs manual.
- Burton 2024 (biplanar native knee): phantom femur MAE 0.22/0.19/0.20° and 0.19/0.25/0.63 mm; manually-tracked femur MAE 0.24/0.49/0.75° and 1.51/0.93/0.33 mm; TF kinematics MAE 0.41/1.07/1.16° and 0.94/0.65/0.66 mm; even in biplanar, the ML axis (least visual change) is the least-sensitive DoF ("movement along this axis corresponds to minimal visual changes in rendered DRRs... less sensitive... as compared to other DoFs"), femur ML consistently below 2 mm.
- ablation.json: runs gain a "benchmarks" block mapping per-axis gaps to these references with a regime tag (single_plane_implant / biplanar_native / ground_truth_type: golden|human_supervised|motion_capture|optotrak) — the runner reports JTML's per-axis numbers next to the applicable field column, so a "0.8 mm in-plane / 6.3 mm z" style result is read against Jensen's 0.8/1.8. Benchmarks are context bands, not gates (ground-truth regime differs; the appearance gate stays the arbiter).
- Caveat: no corpus paper reports golden-pose error on JTML's exact geometry; the closest regime match is Jensen 2023 (same algorithm family, same single-plane implant task). The benchmarks block must carry the regime tag to prevent false equivalence (e.g., Burton's biplanar <1 mm numbers must not be compared to single-plane z gaps without the tag).

#### R3-4 — Perturbation suite mirrors the corpus's gate-like sensitivity analyses

- Flood Table V (dilation sensitivity): method = perturb trunk dilation ±1 and ±2 from high-performance values and re-run the full capture-range experiment; result = femur robust 8-12, tibia 4-8 (Group A) / 6-8 (Group B). Mirror: the suite gains a dilation-robustness sub-table — trunk dilation ∈ {4,5,6,7,8} (JTML's 6 ± 2), record per-variant strict-success/IoU retention; report where JTML's 6 sits relative to the femur band (below it). Flood's caveat — ideal dilation depends on implant pixel size ("a very small implant image (say 64 pixels across) would dilate to meaningless noise") — is the size-dependence check the sub-table must record (JTML Kneel_1 implant pixel size at the actual SID).

- Jensen ambiguous-zone: tibia "2 distinct poses produced roughly identical projections"; blunder = squared-sum rotation diff > 5°; the tibia gate's checked-coverage anchor: the suite's sym-trap injection (mirrored tibia pose) must assert the tibia-after-femur oracle's gate behavior on a ≥5°-class blunder — the gate may legitimately pass the ambiguous pose (identical projection = same IoU), which is exactly why the tibia pass needs the sym-trap pins (R2-3) rather than the appearance gate.
- Yamazaki evaluation curves: per-variable sensitivity curves are the field's version of the z-profile probe; the probe is already the JTML mirror — the corpus confirms the instrument family, not a new instrument.
- Flood's capture-range curve (success ~90% at 4 mm/4° init vs ~50% at 16 mm/16° for conventional methods, from his intro citing [3],[10]) — context for the perturbation suite's Δ magnitudes: the ±{1,2,5,10,15} mm/deg grid brackets exactly the field's success-rate cliff; the minimal-detectable-regression table gains a field-anchored expectation.

### What Could Not Be Verified
- Yamazaki's sweep step width: OCR drops the step number ("ten different points of depth position given [mangled] mm steps") — the 10-point count and ±range behavior are verifiable, the exact step is not.
- Jensen's Table 2/3 per-DoF values: the prose gives in-plane < 0.8 mm / out-of-plane < 1.8 mm / rotations < 1.7°-4°, but the full per-DoF tables are embedded figures in the PDF and were not extractable from the corpus text.

## Round 3 — Lineage and Field Evidence from the Zotero Corpus (measurement-apparatus)

### Summary

Round 3 grounds the apparatus in the algorithm's own lineage, reading the primary texts now in the Zotero corpus. Flood & Banks 2018 (TMI 37(1), DOI 10.1109/TMI.2017.2773398) is the DIRECT-JTA paper the JTML stage loop descends from, and it documents a z-leaf budget of 50,000 evals — equal to the trunk — over a 20 mm out-of-plane range vs 5 mm in-plane, explicitly because out-of-plane translation is "the least accurate degree of freedom for single-plane fluoroscopy": the z-stage budget becomes a first-class manifest parameter and the ablation shapes gain Flood's 50k/3×15k/50k against JTML's 20k/2×5k/5k. Yamazaki 2004 (TMI 23(5), DOI 10.1109/TMI.2004.826051) is a dedicated depth-position remedy paper whose mechanism — build the z evaluation curve, fit a 4th-order polynomial, take its extremum — is the field-validated twin of the z-profile probe, with published depth RMSEs (2.6→0.9 mm simulation, 3.2→1.4 mm in vitro) that become the z-remedies question's external benchmarks and a "difficult to determine a fixed weight" analysis that bears directly on the SAME_Z weight calibration. Modern automatic-registration papers (Jensen 2023 J Arthroplasty; Arulampalam 2025 IJCARS; Burton 2023/2024) supply per-axis error tables for the ablation runner's benchmark blocks, and Flood's dilation/Canny sensitivity tables give the perturbation suite its field-mirroring shape — including the concrete finding that JTML's trunk dilation 6 sits below Flood's femur-robust band (8–12).

### Key Findings

#### R3-1 — Z-leaf budget: the lineage paper allocates 50,000 z-evals (equal to trunk); the z-stage budget becomes a first-class manifest parameter, and the ablation shapes gain Flood's 50k/3×15k/50k
- Primary-text facts (floodAutomatedRegistration3D2018.txt): DIRECT-JTA's stage loop is trunk → three branch restarts → z-translation search: "The iteration budget was 50,000 for the trunk search, 15,000 for each of the three branch searches, and 50,000 for the z-translation search" — the z (leaf-equivalent) budget EQUALS the trunk budget; total 145,000 evals/frame at ~3,000 evals/s on a GTX 970 ("approximately 3,000 iterations per second (50 seconds per frame)"). The z-stage range: "During the z-translation search phase the out-of-plane range was set to 20 mm while all other components were set to 5 mm/degrees." The rationale, verbatim: "This extra search in the out-of-plane translation is necessary because it is the least accurate degree of freedom for single-plane fluoroscopy."
- The JTML mapping (constants verified in Rounds 1–2): trunk 20,000 → 2×branch 5,000 → leaf 5,000 (35k total); leaf ranges (3,3,15,3,3,3) — z 15 mm vs Flood's 20 mm, in-plane 3 vs 5; branch (15,15,25,25,25,25) is verbatim Flood's branch-restart sizing ("15 mm for the in-plane translation, 25 mm for the out-of-plane translation, and 25° for each of the Euler angles"). The z-stage's share of budget: Flood 50k/145k = 34.5%; JTML 5k/35k = 14.3% — a 2.4× lower z-fraction, against the run's load-bearing z-weak-axis problem. Flood also pegged the budget to wall clock ("pegged to take approximately one minute of operating time") — the same pragmatics presumably behind JTML's shape, which is why the budget question must be measured, not argued.
- Spec updates (multi-stage oracle + ablation manifest): (a) budget_shapes gains "flood-direct-jta" {trunk 50000, branch 15000, number_branches 3, leaf 50000} → cumulative caps [50000, 65000, 80000, 95000, 145000], which the stage-bookkeeping gate (costCalls on the cumulative caps) extends to naturally; (b) the z-stage budget becomes an explicit ablation axis z_leaf_budget ∈ {5000 (JTML prod), 20000 (JTML trunk parity), 50000 (Flood parity)}, crossed with the z-range axis {15 mm (JTML), 20 mm (Flood)} — budget and range are separable questions; (c) the dilation schedule axis gains a third reference point: "flood-femur-10-6-1" and "flood-tibia-6-2-1" (Flood: trunk 10 femur / 6 tibia, branch = trunk − 4, z-search 1 — the "decreased by a value of four" scheme), alongside code-6-4-1 and docs-6-3-1; schedule-as-data now has three documented schemes, not two. Note the dilation finding hiding here: JTML's trunk 6 is Flood's TIBIA value — JTML's femur runs the femur at the tibia dilation (see R3-4).
- Per-eval cost context (05-compute-perf boundary): Flood's 145k evals in 50 s implies ~3,000 evals/s; JTML's derived 20–60 evals/s (Round 1, from the flat-3000 "a few minutes") is 50–150× slower per eval — Flood's metric is the GPU-cheap unnormalized L1 on edge images ("L1... can be computed by a GPU extremely efficiently"), JTML's is DRR + dilated-overlap + chamfer per eval. The 50k z-budget is therefore NOT directly transferable; the transfer question is exactly what the Moré & Wild per-stage data profile (R2-4) measures. This is the strongest external anchor yet for Cut 0's per-eval timing record.
- Flood's success-metric decision validates the apparatus's z-gate doctrine: strict success = "within 1 mm for each of the in-plane translations and 1 degree for each of the rotation angles" and "out-of-plane translation is not considered in our definition of success... single-plane, or monocular, radiographic images are extremely unreliable for determining out-of-plane position [10]; this is expected as the translation occurs along the line of sight. An orthogonal biplane comparison is likely the best resolution for this inaccuracy." — the lineage's own answer to z-inaccuracy is biplane (already supported in JTML per Round 1) or the decoupled z-remedy (R3-2); the banded-informational z gate stays correct by the lineage's own measurement convention.
- Confidence: high (primary text, direct quotes; JTML constants source-verified in Rounds 1–2).
- Relevance to this project: turns the "is 5k leaf enough?" question from an argument into a parameterized ablation axis with a lineage-anchored reference shape, and gives the stage-bookkeeping gate a second cumulative-cap vector to assert.

#### R3-2 — Z-profile probe vs the field: Yamazaki 2004's decoupled z-polish is the probe's field twin; its published depth RMSEs (2.6→0.9 mm) are the z-remedies question's benchmarks
- Primary-text facts (yamazakiImprovementDepthPosition2004.txt): the problem statement is verbatim the z-weak axis — "a change in the depth position causes only small changes in the 2-D silhouette"; field accuracy: "the accuracy of the depth position should ideally be about 1 mm, while some researchers report that absolute errors of 2–10 mm have been obtained by computer simulation tests." The mechanism: the z evaluation curve "was more jagged, and the curve peak less pointy" than the other 5 DOF, and its gradient "changed much more markedly with distance" (500/650/850 mm focus distances).
- The documented remedy (the field's z-remedy #1): independent depth optimization. After the conventional 6-DOF registration (Zuffi-style contour + Levenberg–Marquardt), build the z evaluation curve by moving the model along the focus→model-center line at "ten different points" and computing RMSD at each; fit a polynomial; "for fourth- and higher-order polynomials, the extremum error is almost saturated (about 0.5 mm)" → order 4 used; extremum found via Durand–Kerner; then a second conventional registration with the corrected depth. Results: simulation depth RMSE 2.6 mm → 0.9 mm; in vitro 3.2 mm → 1.4 mm; in vivo relative-pose consistency SD 4.9 mm → 1.5 mm; the other 5 DOF unchanged (SD ≈ 0.1 mm translations, ≈ 0.2–0.3° rotations). Residual: ~0.5 mm average z bias, "thought to be caused by slight errors in translation parallel to fluoroscopic images" — in-plane error couples INTO z.
- The field's other documented z remedies, now corpus-backed: (2) biplane — Flood "an orthogonal biplane comparison is likely the best resolution"; Yamazaki: biplane reports exist but "limited space for testing, system complexity and increased radiation exposure remain unresolved" (already supported in JTML, Round 1); (3) known-geometry prior — "conventional techniques assumed that there is no displacement between the femoral and tibial components on lateral images... depth position was ignored, and relative medio-lateral translation was set to zero" (JTML already pins the tibia relative to femur from .jts — the prior is built in); (4) penalized z — Jensen 2023: tibia optimization "included additional mediolateral translation and varus/valgus rotation penalties" (the field precedent for JTML's pole-constraint family, and its SAME_Z weight).
- Probe spec updates: (a) "yamazaki-polynomial mode" — on the SAME 31-render sweep (zero extra renders), fit a 4th-order polynomial (robust least squares) and report poly_argmin_mm + fit residual alongside the raw argmin and valley_depth; this is a drop-in, field-validated z-remedy candidate (10 points in Yamazaki, 31 here) that the polish stage (angle 06) can consume as its z-arm; (b) "fixed-weight evidence" — Yamazaki on the SAME_Z-type calibration: "a weighted optimization is generally applied to compensate for the difference of variable scale, [but] it would be difficult to determine a fixed weight value... because of the difference in gradient for each evaluation curve", and the z gradient changes with focus distance — the SAME_Z weight is fighting a distance-dependent scale; the probe must record the z-valley gradient at JTML's actual focus distance (JT_INTCALIB 1198 mm principal distance, angle-06 calibration) and the ablation should compare SAME_Z-weighted vs decoupled (Yamazaki-style) z-polish rather than SAME_Z alone; (c) "coupling mode" — re-run the sweep at ± the minimal-detectable-regression in-plane Δ (R2-1's table) to measure dz*/d(in-plane), the mechanism behind Yamazaki's residual bias; this upgrades probe assertion p4 (z_gap anti-correlates with valley_depth) from correlation to mechanism.
- The z-remedies question, answered with a band: the field's single-plane depth-position accuracy spans Yamazaki conventional 2.6–3.2 mm RMSE → remedied 0.9–1.4 mm, Jensen (DIRECT-JTA lineage) out-of-plane < 1.8 mm RMS vs human-supervised, Arulampalam depth MAE 1.8 mm (R3-3). JTML's measured 6.31 mm (frame 1, flat-3000 shape) sits at the top of Yamazaki's reported 2–10 mm range and ~3.5× above the lineage's own 1.8 mm — a candidate regression against the lineage, with two honest caveats: JTML's gap is vs the fem.jts golden (not human-supervised) at a trunk-only flat-3000 shape that NEVER runs the leaf z-stage, and the production shape may shrink it. The multi-stage oracle + probe are exactly the instruments that decide.
- Confidence: high on the Yamazaki facts (primary text); medium on the JTML-vs-field comparison (different ground-truth regimes and shapes — the caveats above are the honest framing).
- Relevance: gives the z-remedy decision (synthesis recommendation 8's GO condition) a field-validated remedy to test (decoupled polynomial z-polish), an external accuracy band to report against, and a mechanism (in-plane→z coupling) for the probe to measure.

#### R3-3 — State-of-the-art benchmarks: per-axis external error tables for the ablation runner's reports
- Corpus-sourced numbers, the applicable columns for the runner's benchmark block:
  - Jensen 2023 (jensenJointTrackMachine2023.txt — the dispatch's "jensenAutonomousMethodExtracting2021" citekey maps here; J Arthroplasty, the 2021 preprint's published form): RMS vs human-supervised — in-plane translations < 0.8 mm, out-of-plane < 1.8 mm, rotations ≤ 4° inside the tibial ambiguous zone / < 1.7° outside; external validation (45 instrumented-sawbones motion-capture frames + 260 single-plane image pairs from a biplane study): "All in-plane translation errors were submillimeter, except S/I from the biplane fluoroscopic study. All rotation errors were <1.8°"; blunder threshold = squared-sum rotation difference > 5°. Method note: CNN segmentation → NFD shape-library initial pose → DIRECT-JTA refinement, "the leaf branch served to find the optimal out-of-plane translation" — the same stage-loop family as JTML, and its out-of-plane note is the field confirming the z-weak axis inside the lineage itself: "Due to poor sensitivity for measuring out-of-plane translation with monocular vision, the medio-lateral translation had the largest RMS differences", and "the out-of-plane translation estimates were relatively poor... extremely sensitive to model projection and edge detection details".
  - Flood 2018: strict success = in-plane ≤ 1 mm AND rotations ≤ 1° (out-of-plane excluded by definition); "average out-of-plane translation around one millimeter" for femur at convergence-range trials; capture range ±55 mm/deg femur, ±25–40 tibia (tibia limited by a symmetric-trap local minimum "just over a degree along the Y Euler angle" — the sym-trap lineage).
  - Yamazaki 2004: z 2.6→0.9 mm sim / 3.2→1.4 mm in vitro; other 5 DOF SD ≈ 0.1 mm / ≈ 0.2–0.3°.
  - Arulampalam 2025 (arulampalamAccuracyNovelAutomated2025.txt, IJCARS, DOI 10.1007/s11548-025-03389-y — automated 2D-3D for THA cup from single-plane intraoperative fluoroscopy): MAE 1.9° inclination [−4.4, 4.8], 1.5° anteversion [−7.3, 4.1], 1.6 mm height [−5, 3.8], 1.8 mm depth [−7.3, 4.1]; 100% inclination within 5°, 98% anteversion within 5°, 90% height within 3 mm, 81% depth within 3 mm — depth is the weakest axis even in a 2025 automated product.
  - Burton 2023 (burtonFullyAutomaticTracking2023.txt, CBM 163:107189, DOI 10.1016/j.compbiomed.2023.107189 — biplanar native glenohumeral): median orientation 1.7° scapula / 8.6° humerus vs manual tracking.
  - Burton 2024 (burtonFullyAutomaticTracking2024.txt, J Biomech 166:112066, DOI 10.1016/j.jbiomech.2024.112066 — biplanar native knee): phantom femur MAE 0.22/0.19/0.20° rotation and 0.19/0.25/0.63 mm translation; manually-tracked femur MAE 0.24/0.49/0.75° and 1.51/0.93/0.33 mm; TF kinematics MAE 0.41/1.07/1.16° and 0.94/0.65/0.66 mm; and the z-weak-axis fact survives even in biplanar: "movement along this axis corresponds to minimal visual changes in rendered DRRs... the pose refinement loss landscape is less sensitive to changes in this DoF", femur ML consistently below 2 mm.
- Spec updates: ablation.json runs gain a "benchmarks" block: per-axis recovered-vs-golden gaps tagged with regime (single_plane_implant / biplanar_native; ground_truth_type ∈ golden|human_supervised|motion_capture|optotrak|phantom) and the applicable field column(s); the runner's summary line reports e.g. "in-plane 0.8 mm / z 6.3 mm vs Jensen 0.8/1.8 (single_plane_implant, human_supervised)". Benchmarks are context bands, never gates — the appearance gate stays the arbiter, and the regime tag prevents false equivalence (Burton's biplanar <1 mm numbers must not be compared to single-plane z gaps without the tag). Closest regime match for JTML's task: Jensen 2023 (same algorithm family, same single-plane implant task); Flood 2018 for the strict-success convention.
- Confidence: high (all numbers primary-text; regime caveats explicit in the schema).
- Relevance: the ablation runner's reports stop being bare IoU/L1/z numbers and become comparisons the run's decision-makers can read against the field — including the honest position that JTML's measured 6.31 mm z gap is ~3.5× the lineage's own out-of-plane RMS.

#### R3-4 — Perturbation suite mirrors the corpus's gate-like sensitivity analyses
- Flood 2018 Table V (dilation sensitivity) — the exact shape to mirror: perturb the trunk dilation ±1 and ±2 from the high-performance values and re-run the full capture-range experiment; result: "the femur implants are relatively robust at trunk dilations of eight to twelve, while the Group A tibial implants performed well at dilation levels of four to eight. The Group B tibial implants favored a higher dilation in the range of six to eight." Suite upgrade: the perturbation suite (R2-1) gains a dilation-robustness sub-table — trunk dilation ∈ {4, 5, 6, 7, 8} (= JTML's 6 ± 2), recording per-variant strict-success retention / IoU, with the report line "JTML trunk 6 sits BELOW the femur-robust band (8–12) and at the tibia band's low edge (4–8)". Flood's size caveat — "the ideal dilation values are likely to also depend on the size of the implant in pixels. A very small implant image (say 64 pixels across) would dilate to meaningless noise" — is the size-dependence check the sub-table must record for Kneel_1's implant pixel size at the actual SID.
- Flood 2018 Table VI (Canny sensitivity) — two directions, not one: "highly noisy" (too-sensitive thresholds, 20/65 and 30/80 per group) vs "insufficient edge detection" (too-insensitive, 40/100 and 100/140). Suite upgrade: INJ-EDGE becomes Flood's two-directional pair (one noisy-threshold config, one insensitive config), asserting the gate trips in both directions or recording which direction it is blind to.
- Jensen 2023 ambiguous-zone analysis — the tibia gate's checked-coverage anchor: "Transversely symmetric tibial implants posed problems during registration because 2 distinct poses produced roughly identical projections"; blunder = squared-sum rotation difference > 5°; and the remedy ordering "the tibial implant was always optimized after the nonsymmetric femoral implant" (the field precedent for JTML's tibia-after-femur, R2-3). Suite implication: the sym-trap injection (mirrored tibia pose) may legitimately PASS the appearance gate — identical projection ≈ identical IoU, by definition of the ambiguity — so the tibia pass's checked coverage lives in the sym-trap pins (launch directive == "Sym_Trap", relay count == 60, costCalls == 20000), not the IoU gate; the suite asserts the pins trip, not the gate.
- Yamazaki 2004 per-variable evaluation curves: the field's own gate-like sensitivity analysis is a per-DoF curve family — the z-profile probe IS the JTML mirror of this instrument; corpus confirms the instrument family, no new instrument needed.
- Flood's intro capture-range curve — context for the suite's Δ magnitudes: conventional registration success "can be around 90% when the initial guess is 4mm from the in-plane solution, and 4° from the rotation solution... [but] can drop to as low as 50% when the initial guess is within 16mm and 16°" — the ±{1,2,5,10,15} mm/deg grid of R2-1 brackets exactly the field's success-rate cliff; the minimal-detectable-regression table gains a field-anchored expectation for where the cliff should appear.
- Confidence: high (all primary-text; the suite upgrades are direct mirrors).
- Relevance: the perturbation suite's checked-coverage argument (R2-1) is no longer first-principles-only — every injection class now has a corpus-documented sensitivity experiment it mirrors, and the dilation sub-table converts a doc-contradiction (6/3/1 vs 6/4/1) into a measured robustness band with a lineage reference.

## Task summary

**Deliverable**: Appended `## Round 3 — Lineage and Field Evidence from the Zotero Corpus` to `angles/03-measurement-apparatus.org` via `panoptes_write_artifact` (append=true), read-only otherwise.

**What Round 3 contains** (all four deepening tasks, evidence from primary corpus texts):

1. **Z-leaf budget (R3-1)** — Flood & Banks 2018 (TMI) is the DIRECT-JTA lineage paper: z-leaf budget **50,000 evals = trunk**, range **20 mm z vs 5 mm in-plane**, with the verbatim rationale "the least accurate degree of freedom for single-plane fluoroscopy". The multi-stage oracle spec now treats the z-stage budget as a first-class manifest parameter (`z_leaf_budget ∈ {5000, 20000, 50000}` crossed with z-range {15, 20} mm), ablation shapes gain **Flood's 50k/3×15k/50k** vs JTML's 20k/2×5k/5k (z-fraction 34.5% vs 14.3%), and the dilation axis gains "flood-femur-10-6-1"/"flood-tibia-6-2-1" reference points. Also: Flood's success metric excludes out-of-plane (validates the banded-informational z-gate doctrine), and Flood's 3,000 evals/s vs JTML's derived 20–60 evals/s quantifies the per-eval cost gap (05 boundary).
2. **Z-profile probe vs the field (R3-2)** — Yamazaki 2004 documents the decoupled z-polish remedy: z evaluation curve → 4th-order polynomial fit (extremum error saturates ~0.5 mm) → independent depth optimization; results **2.6→0.9 mm (sim), 3.2→1.4 mm (in vitro), 4.9→1.5 mm (in vivo)**, residual ~0.5 mm bias from in-plane→z coupling. Field depth-accuracy band: 1 mm ideal, 2–10 mm reported. The probe gains three modes: yamazaki-polynomial, fixed-weight evidence (Yamazaki: "difficult to determine a fixed weight" — directly informs SAME_Z), and in-plane-coupling. JTML's 6.31 mm gap sits ~3.5× above the lineage's own 1.8 mm out-of-plane RMS (Jensen 2023), framed with honest caveats (golden-vs-human-supervised, trunk-only shape).
3. **State-of-the-art benchmarks (R3-3)** — Jensen 2023 (in-plane < 0.8 mm / out-of-plane < 1.8 mm / rotations < 1.7°–4°), Arulampalam 2025 (MAE 1.9°/1.5°/1.6 mm/1.8 mm; depth weakest axis even in 2025), Burton 2023 (1.7°/8.6° median biplanar GH), Burton 2024 (phantom femur 0.19–0.63 mm / 0.20–0.22°; ML least-sensitive even in biplanar), Flood strict-success convention. ablation.json gains a regime-tagged `benchmarks` block (context bands, never gates).
4. **Perturbation suite mirror (R3-4)** — Flood Table V (dilation robustness: femur 8–12, tibia 4–8) → dilation-robustness sub-table with the concrete finding that **JTML's trunk dilation 6 sits below Flood's femur-robust band**; Flood Table VI → two-directional INJ-EDGE; Jensen ambiguous-zone/blunder (5°) → tibia checked-coverage lives in the sym-trap pins, not the IoU gate; Yamazaki evaluation curves = the probe's field twin.
